hints: Focus on statement 1 and think about where haemoglobinic acid forms: in respiring tissues where oxyhaemoglobin is unloading its oxygen, not where it is loading oxygen.
Recall what carbonic anhydrase does inside red blood cells: CO2 + H2O to carbonic acid to H+ + hydrogencarbonate, and ask what happens to that H+ when oxygen leaves haemoglobin.
walkthrough:
**Picture what happens in respiring tissues**

Think of blood arriving at an active tissue full of oxyhaemoglobin. Here oxygen dissociates to diffuse into cells: $Hb(O_2)_4 \rightarrow Hb + 4O_2$. Only this deoxygenated haemoglobin, Hb, is free to pick up hydrogen ions to form haemoglobinic acid, $Hb + H^+ \rightarrow HHb$. So statement 1 is true.

**Link carbonic anhydrase to the H+ supply**

In the same red blood cell, CO2 from respiration enters and carbonic anhydrase speeds up: $$CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$$ That $H^+$ is exactly what combines with the deoxygenated Hb from Step 1 to make HHb. So formation of haemoglobinic acid is directly linked to carbonic anhydrase action, and statement 3 is true.

**See why this is brilliant buffering**

If those $H^+$ ions stayed free in plasma, blood pH would fall and become too acidic. By mopping them up as HHb, a weak acid, haemoglobin removes excess $H^+$ and keeps pH stable. So statement 2 is true, and 1 + 2 + 3 gives option A.

options.A: Correct, because all three statements are true: HHb needs deoxygenated Hb, it buffers H+ from the carbonic anhydrase reaction, and so prevents acidosis.
options.B: Incomplete, because it leaves out statement 3 which is true, since the H+ that forms HHb comes from carbonic acid made by carbonic anhydrase.
options.C: Incomplete, because statements 2 and 3 are also true, HHb formation is an important buffer linked to CO2 transport.
options.D: Incomplete, because it leaves out statement 1 which is true, only haemoglobin that has released oxygen can accept H+ to become HHb.
